sections.title: Raf: getting the foundations right
paragraphs: Raf aligned our understanding of tokens, context, orchestrators, harnesses, agents and skills.
items: AI hasn’t replaced the fundamentals: hand-coding, thinking and collaboration still matter for productivity.
Skills are built for agents. They compose and load progressively.
A Glossary.md can help manage context.

sections.title: Mash: putting skills into practice
paragraphs: Mash gave a live demo using Matt Pocock’s skills on a real online shop project, adding a Favourites feature to show how skills can help identify, investigate, implement and resolve tickets and issues.
items: Third-party skills: be wary of prompt injection when using them.
Choosing models: models aren’t bad anymore, so there’s less need to agonise over which one to use.
Hooks, guardrails and sandboxing: Mash explained pre- and post-hooks, and why you should sandbox AI so it can’t go rogue and delete things on your machine.
Build skills for your own context: custom skills are a must for tailoring agents to how you work.

title: Tales from the USA: AI and Tech Insights
summary: A panel compared AI product development and technology work in the United States and Perth.
imageAlt: Panellists Alex Bertram, Tim de Boer and Raj Saddi speaking at the Tales from the USA event.
artworkAlt: Tales from the USA panel event artwork featuring Alex Bertram, Tim de Boer and Raj Saddi.

paragraphs: We were extremely grateful to have
, and
join our interactive panel session to discuss what they learned about opportunities, market dynamics, and cultural differences between working in the US and Perth.
Alex is General Manager – Americas at Greenroom Robotics, a maritime autonomy company. A former Perth local, he’s back in Perth for a short visit.

Tim de Boer is Founder and CEO of Interfuze and Raj Saddi is a principal consultant, both with a long history in Perth’s IT industry. Tim and Raj recently travelled to San Francisco for AI Engineer World Fair. Tim also spent time in SF back in 2000 on the roll out of the city’s Australian built transit system.

sections.title: Panel highlight
paragraphs: This panel landed the real story: the US is moving fast on AI product execution, while Perth is strong on quality and governance. The call to action was clear — build locally, test monetization early, and learn from the cultural difference in customer expectations.

sections.title: Takeaways from our panel
items: 🔹 AI engineering is now its own discipline — jargon, norms, and a "100mph" sharing culture across founders, enterprises, and universities.
🔹 Teams are shrinking to pods: PM + lead + AI agents, with senior engineers shipping solo and facing customers directly. Failure cases now matter more than wins.
🔹 The bottleneck has flipped — building is easy, code volume is exploding. Efficiency, not output, is becoming the real differentiator.

🔹 US vs AU gap isn't really about tech — it's mindset. The US dives in; Australia hesitates on governance and risk. Meanwhile our liability and data rules (especially in health/education) are genuinely stricter and slower to move.
🔹 This isn't a bubble, it's a gearshift. Expertise is accessible in months, not years — we're standing on the shoulders of giants and accelerating fast.
🔹 Best advice from the room: go see it firsthand (SF, or a regional hub like Singapore if budget's tight), and start testing monetization now — the "how do we build it" question is basically solved.

paragraphs: AIE is heading to Sydney next — worth watching for anyone who missed SF.
Thanks to everyone who spent their evening with us and all the questions! Thanks for watching the photo slide-show and taking the ‘who’s who’ quiz!!

sections.title: Why it mattered
paragraphs: This session wasn’t just about US stories — it was about showing Perth how quickly the global AI landscape is moving, and why local founders should keep one eye on execution speed while staying grounded on risk and customer trust.

sections.title: Silly Pitch descriptions
items: ) — An AI agent that hunts down governments handing out "silly grants." The pitch was pure performance — Luca stripped off his top and belt just to grab the room. The idea itself? That was the punchline: there wasn't one. All hustle, no product.

) — Emotional blackmail as a fitness app. Snaps a guilty photo of you skipping the gym and threatens to send your "dirty laundry" to family and friends if you don't go. Biggest risk: getting hacked and having your own laundry leaked back at you. Competitor: Snapchat. Already planning an enterprise tier and "going IPO" on one person's yes.

) — A brain-implanted AI that says "no" for you — silently. Plant a chip, let the AI live in your head, and it beams a wave straight to the other person's brain so they get their answer without you saying a word. Monetization: pay per message.

) — An AI trained to predict the exact moment your pet's about to do something silly, so you can catch it, go viral, and monetize the fame. Biggest blocker: owning a pet that's actually well-behaved. Silly fish, though? That's money.

) — A rating-and-challenge app for the worst food combinations imaginable. Rate the horrors, challenge friends to top them, monetize via brands brave enough to sponsor the chaos. Ethos: embrace disgust.
) — A marketplace for celebrity look-alikes — because real celebrities are too expensive, but a Matthew McConaughey look-alike is a bargain. Monetized via tokens and API credits.

title: Aura Ventures Mixer
summary: Perth's startup scene came alive at the historic Print Hall last month, as Aura Ventures — a Sydney-based VC firm backing the next generation of global technology companies — touched down in WA to connect with the local innovation community. The evening was a collaboration with Build Club Perth, bringing together the best of both networks under one roof.
imageAlt: Perth founders and visitors meeting at the Aura Ventures mixer.

sections.title: 🤝 VCs Meet Perth's Ecosystem
paragraphs: Aura Group Managing Director Eric Chan and Partner Mark Esterhuizen hosted an evening of drinks and conversation for Perth's founders, investors, and operators. Over 40 people from across the ecosystem showed up to meet the Sydney visitors, swap ideas, and see what's moving in both the Perth and broader Australian tech landscape.

sections.title: ✨ The Venue
paragraphs: The venue set the tone — Print Hall is Perth doing what it does best, blending character with a bit of quiet confidence.

Marcus Tan

Matt James

paragraphs: It was great to see founders like Ryan Liebregts (Indrus) in the mix alongside students Issy Ng and Jay Nicholson, and Perth Angels — a reminder that the ecosystem here spans every stage.

paragraphs: A big thanks to Annie Liao, Saanvi Yearawar, and Sabrina for pulling the night together, and to Aura Ventures for the generous hospitality. Nights like this are exactly how ecosystems grow — one conversation at a time.
